_![Image 1: Title Screen](https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/a/review/24/172524-1.png)_

_Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2_ is a skateboarding game by Vicarious Visions for the Game Boy Advance, a handheld port of the original Neversoft-developed Playstation game, both published by Activision. One of the launch titles for the GBA in the US, this _THPS2_ port was designed to showcase the relative power of the new handheld system, delivering an experience much more similar to the console versions than the earlier, duly forgotten Game Boy Color games in the series, which played more closely to 8-bit games like _720 Degrees_ or _Skate or_ Die than the real deal _._ But while handheld aficionados of the time were quite impressed with the translation, this version of _THPS2_ is nonetheless a lousy substitute for the classic console versions and borderline unplayable by comparison: while someone only exposed to this version might be able to squeeze a few ounces of fun out of it, anyone coming from one of the console games will surely be disappointed.

The premise of the console game is intact: guide the pro skater of your choice around the various environments performing tricks and collecting items and cash within a time limit in order to knock out the various level goals, with some levels being pure competition courses. But only something like half of the game is here: only 5 of the levels appear (plus the warehouse one from the original _Pro Skater_) and the multiplayer, create-a-character option, and park editors are all absent. If all other aspects of the game were intact, that means we're talking about less than an hour of playtime for a career mode runthrough, with more only if you're going for the gap checklist or trying to unlock stuff by running through the game with everyone. Of course, unsurprisingly, very few of the game's other aspects are intact.

![Image 2: In-Game 1](https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/a/review/24/172524-2.png)

For starters, there's the game's awkward perspective. In order to allow the Game Boy Advance, a handheld with tech levels comparable to a Super Nintendo, to host a Playstation game, some serious changes had to made to the visual design of the game. While your skater is still a polygonal character (although simpler and more abstract looking, which is fine due to the smaller screen), the game is no longer played from a 3D perspective, instead adopting an isometric one. The game's stages are mostly intact with some alterations, but they're now displayed in a fixed, pre-rendered manner. This perspective works great for games where precision character movements aren't a necessity, like in turn-based or real-time strategy games, but for a fast-paced action game like this, it makes it unnecessarily difficult to perform once simple tasks like lining up jumps or grinds or seeing what you're doing when your view is blocked by objects in the foreground. Since you can't see any further than your immediate surroundings, it's much more difficult to find all the little items scattered throughout the air (good luck finding the secret tapes or the cash icons here!) or even the full extents of the levels. The pre-rendered environments also lack the interactivity of the console ones, so you'll no longer be opening up doors to secret areas or dodging traffic or anything like that.

There's also the awkward control, thanks to the GBA's button layout. Since there are only half the face and shoulder buttons available, all the console versions' moves have to be translated into a more concise setup. Remarkably, tricking mechanics mostly work like they're supposed to, with flips and grinds and manuals and grabs and even special moves all working roughly the way they do on console, but I found it awkward to have to rely on the shoulder buttons for basic tricks so much here. I don't know if they could have possibly made it any easier given the button layout they were working with here, but it really is difficult to play compared to the originals and makes you wonder if they should have simply left the entire idea of porting this on the cutting room floor.

![Image 3: In-Game 2](https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/a/review/24/172524-3.png)

Because it's a cartridge and not a CD, the GBA port also has a vastly different, shorter soundtrack, ranging from crude but inoffensive instrumental hip hop beats to unpleasantly noisy rock-esque VGMs, none of which are enjoyable. The graphics are overall blurry and unimpressive and, though the game has no loading times and has little in motion to actually render onscreen, it still somehow suffers from slowdown in the busier moments.

While it's admirable that they attempted to translate as much as they did from the proper game to this handheld version, there's still so much of what made the Playstation Tony Hawk games great that is missing here that this cannot possibly be recommended to anyone in the present day, especially with so many other competent ports, sequels, knock-offs and remakes out there.
